newsitem.title: MEXICO: Peru hostage crisis highlights risk for investors.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis highlights risk for investors.

text.p: The siege by leftist guerrillas in Peru Wednesday was the latest shock for investors who have had to stomach rebel attacks, assassinations and devaluations as they sought fat returns in Latin America.
Those who had bet on the economic and political success story of Peru under President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s Wednesday became victims of a classic Latin American "bump in the night."

Hundreds of partygoers at a glittery reception in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, Peru, were taken hostage by communist guerrillas late on Tuesday, marking a revival of a threat investors long had believed Fujimori had crushed.

The guerrillas from the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement threatened to kill up to 490 hostages in the ambassador's residence late Wednesday as hopes for a quick breakthrough faded a day after the building was stormed.

"You just panic, you try to reduce your risk," said Gary Evans, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers in New York, explaining the reaction of investors early Wednesday to a country that until recently was a favourite among the so-called emerging economies in Latin American and elsewhere.

As traders pushed sell buttons, the Peruvian Stock Exchange suspended trading, facing losses of over 4 percent in its main index. That was a double blow for investors, who were left with no escape route in their scramble to get out.

According to Evans, battle-hardened traders long used to the ups and downs of Latin America's fickle markets saw buying opportunities as their more jittery counterparts fled. But whether their optimism was merely fleeting depended largely on the outcome of the siege.
"Is this going to change the fundamental paradigm in Peru? Is this a major threat to the government? The jury is still out, but I don't think so," Evans said.
One thing was clear, however. Latin America in the last three years has been no picnic for foreign investors chasing fast returns.
Almost exactly two years ago, a surpise overnight peso devaluation in Mexico thrust much of Latin America into an economic spiral from which it is still struggling to emerge.

Investors in New York heckled and jeered the Mexican finance minister at the time as he sought to explain how in a few tragic days before Christmas 1994 he had wiped billions of dollars off the value of their investments.

If Mexico's economy has rebounded from the crisis this year, its stock market remains at pre-crisis levels in dollar terms. One reason: leftist guerrillas in Mexico, who were shrugged off by investors and the government as a farse until they launched bloody overnight attacks in late August.

The abrupt resignation in July of Domingo Cavallo, architect of Argentina's economic resurgence, guerrilla attacks in Colombia, and the resurgence of the rebel movement in Peru have helped tarnish Latin America's image as a reform-bent region that was a gold mine for investors.
Some analysts said the perils were only now becoming fully understood.
"We've been in an extended bear market in Latin America for what amounts to three years," said Ernest Brown, economist at New York investment bank Morgan Stanley.
"Anyone who's invested is not all starry-eyed by the opportunities. They weigh the risk and after three years, the skittish money has been shaken out."

While investors in Peru may weather the storm, some analysts were ringing warning bells over Latin America in general, saying the persisent sluggishness of the region's economies was breeding "reform fatigue" among citizens unable to escape poverty. That could translate into unrest.

"We perceive the beginning of a disenchantment with the reform process in many countries," Lehman Brothers' Evans wrote in a recent report. "Though not yet translated into a major or cohesive political movement, the minor change in sentiment increases the event risk in many emerging market countries."
